name: Sam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the child benefit processing team at the benefits office in town, on the second floor behind the post room. A lot of claims still come in on paper, so I check the forms, match birth certificates, key everything into the system and chase anything missing. I'm a year and a half in and my error rate's still higher than it should be, which my team leader Ruth mentions at every review. It's not exciting, but I like knowing what tomorrow looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, in a good way. I bought a one-bed flat two years ago with help from my parents, so the mortgage is small and I've got savings on top. Five-a-side on Thursdays, Sunday dinner at my mum's. My uncle Luis has a tiling business and keeps saying I should join him, but I like a desk and a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Every year there's something new that's supposed to change everything, and then it's mostly the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it like it is: it's a tool, it does some bits, life goes on. I don't really talk about work online. At five-a-side I'd probably just say 'told you'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the routine bits it takes might be my bits. Keying in paper forms is about as routine as it gets. If the scanner starts reading the forms itself, I'm not sure what I'd be doing on a Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on my error rate, because that's the one thing Ruth keeps raising. I'd ask to shadow someone on the phone team in case they move people over. And I'd keep saving like normal, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Nothing dramatic, but it's on my mind more than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything like that already started at your office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scanner already reads some of the newer forms, and nobody told us until it was running. One week I just had fewer forms in my tray. Nobody lost their job, but I noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money? Anything you'd change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. It's all fine. Small mortgage, my parents nearby, money in the bank. It's the job I'd worry about, not the bills.

say: It's **a tool**, it does some bits, and life goes on.
I'd say **'told you'** at five-a-side and leave it there.
think: Keying in paper forms is the **routine work** AI takes first.
I'm not sure what I'd **do on a Monday** without it.
do: **Cut my error rate** before the next review.
Ask to **shadow the phone team** in case people move over.
Keep **saving a bit more** than usual.
feel: **Uneasy**, more than I'd admit to anyone.
S0.quote: One week I just had fewer forms in my tray. Nobody lost their job, but I noticed.
fieldNote: Even the plateau touches him because his day is **routine keying**.
He says calm things in public but **privately counts forms**.
Money is **solid**; the job is the worry.

steps.text: Cut the error rate on child benefit keying before the review
Ask to shadow the phone team for a few days
Put an extra £100 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one where my job goes, isn't it? Checking forms is exactly the checking it's talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but it's progress, and you can't stop it. At work I'd keep my head down. I'm not the type to make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm one of the first. Junior, mistakes on my record, and I don't use the tools. If they cut the processing team from ten to four, I'm not in the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a move to the phone team or the face-to-face appointments, where you need to talk people through things. I'd keep my savings and not touch them. And I'd probably have a proper conversation with my uncle Luis about tiling, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like knowing what tomorrow looks like, and suddenly I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the AI tools to stay in the four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I know I should, but I've seen people spend ages getting it to do something they could've just done. If they made me, I'd learn it. I just wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the appeal of tiling, if you'd rather stay at a desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays, it's work with your hands, and a robot isn't tiling bathrooms soon. My uncle's busy every week. I just don't want to give up the pension and the regular hours.

say: It's a shame, but it's **progress**; you can't stop it.
At work I'd **keep my head down**, not make speeches.
think: If the team goes **from ten to four**, I'm not in the four.
I'm junior, **make mistakes**, and don't use the tools.
do: Ask to move to the **phone team** or appointments.
Leave the **savings untouched** as a buffer.
Talk to my uncle about **tiling** as a backup.
S1.quote: If they cut the processing team from ten to four, I'm not in the four.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **first to go** and says so plainly.
He'd learn AI only **if made to**.
His uncle's **tiling business** is a backup he doesn't want.

steps.text: Ask to move from processing to the phone team
Leave the savings untouched as a buffer
Talk to uncle Luis about tiling work as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not much time to do anything. That's basically next Christmas but one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope the government's got a plan, because nobody else will. To mates, I'd keep it light. But I'd be saying it to my mum more than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the whole processing floor is gone by 2028, me included. Even the phone team, because it answers people better than us. I don't know what's left for someone like me in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle Luis and start learning tiling properly, maybe evenings and Saturdays first. Robots are three years behind, so that's a few years of work. I'd keep the savings for the gap and not take any holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat if things go badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably sell the flat eventually, if it came to it. But not first. First the savings, then the car, then the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like a desk and a pension. How does leaving that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sad, but you go where the work is. A desk doesn't matter if the desk is gone.

say: I hope **the government** has a plan, because nobody else will.
I'd keep it light with mates but **talk to my mum**.
think: The **whole processing floor** goes by 2028, me included.
I don't know what's left for **someone like me**.
do: **Learn tiling** with my uncle on evenings and Saturdays.
S2.quote: A desk doesn't matter if the desk is gone.
fieldNote: Fast AGI pushes him into the **hands-on backup** he resisted.
He has a clear order: **savings, car, flat**.
He trusts **government** to have the plan, not himself.

steps.text: Learn tiling with uncle Luis on evenings and Saturdays
Skip holidays and keep spending tight
Keep the savings untouched for the gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast, but I'd be thirty-two, not twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming so let's be sensible about it. I'd probably say it to Ruth, actually: what's the plan for the processing team? I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job goes, just later. The extra time doesn't save it. It just means I can't pretend I didn't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for a couple of years and see who they keep. If it's clear we're going, by year two I'd start tiling with my uncle part-time. And I'd pay down the mortgage with some savings, so I'm not stuck with it if the money changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay down the mortgage rather than keep the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a smaller mortgage means I can earn less and still be fine. My dad paid off the house when his factory shut, then went to the bus depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years make you more likely to commit to tiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd take tiling more seriously, maybe a proper course at the college. Five years is long enough to finish one.

say: It's coming, so let's **be sensible** about it and not shout.
I'd ask my team leader: **what's the plan** for processing?
think: The **job goes later**, not never; extra time doesn't save it.
I **can't pretend** I didn't know what was coming.
do: **Keep working** two years and see who stays.
**Pay down the mortgage** with some savings.
S3.quote: My dad paid off the house when his factory shut, then went to the bus depot.
fieldNote: He copies **his father's playbook**: clear the house, then switch.
He **waits first**, true to his nature, then moves.
Five years lets him **finish a course**.

steps.text: Wait two years to see who the processing team keeps
Pay a chunk of savings off the mortgage
Take a tiling course at the college by year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like a long way off. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so no need to panic. Let's see how it goes. That's probably what most people at the office would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait too long. That's me. But I'd know the job ends, and I'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office, work on getting better, and maybe move to the phone team. I'd start Saturdays with my uncle around year three or four, just to keep it open. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slow way. The job is safe for now, but it's not my job for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get you to move earlier than you'd naturally want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want somebody to tell me. Like Ruth, or the union. If they said 'start now', I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tiling turned out to be your real job by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be alright, I think. My uncle Luis has been tiling for thirty years and has never had a quiet month.

say: There's time, so **no need to panic**.
Let's **see how it goes**, like most people at the office.
think: I'd probably **wait too long**; that's just how I am.
The job **isn't for life**, and I know it.
do: **Stay at the office** and try for the phone team.
**Start Saturdays tiling** around year three or four.
feel: **Slow anxiety**: safe now, but not **for life**.
S4.quote: My uncle Luis has been tiling for thirty years and has never had a quiet month.
fieldNote: He admits he'll **wait too long**, then asks for a nudge.
Ten years makes **tiling** feel like a real fallback.
He'd act if his **team leader** or union said so.

steps.text: Stay at the benefits office and apply for the phone team
Start Saturdays tiling with uncle Luis around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. I wouldn't have time to learn a trade before the job went. What would help is someone, the department or the union, telling us straight what's happening to processing and paying for a proper course in something hands-on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how boring people like me are. Not everyone wants to change. Some of us just want a steady job and Sunday dinner at our mum's.

headlineQuote: Not everyone wants to change. Some of us just want a steady job and Sunday dinner at our mum's.
portrait: A **27-year-old child benefit processor**, keying paper claims with an error rate he's working on.
He likes **routine and a pension**, never uses AI, and owns a flat with family help.
Even the plateau unsettles him because his work is **routine keying**.
In the AGI scenarios he turns to **tiling with his uncle**, a backup he never wanted.
He knows he'd **wait too long** and wants someone to tell him when to move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade first.
whatWouldHelp: **Straight answers** from the department or union about the processing team.
A paid **hands-on course** for people whose desk jobs go.
